mis.m: Counts forward smoothly but gets stuck or skips numbers when crossing from 12 to 13 or from 19 to 20, for example saying '11, 12, 15'.
mis.why: The teen number names are irregular and do not sound like 'ten-three' or 'ten-four', so the pattern is hard to hear.
mis.fix: Count teens with a full ten frame plus loose counters, saying 'ten and three, thirteen' as each counter is added.

mis.m: Counting backward from 15, says '15, 14, 13, 12, 11, 10, 9' but then restarts forward or says '9, 10'.
mis.why: Backward counting is less practiced, and students fall back on the familiar forward sequence.
mis.fix: Use a number path on the floor and have students walk backward one step for each number, touching each numeral as they say it.

mis.m: Says the number words in order but moves objects faster or slower than the words, so the count does not match the set.
mis.why: One-to-one matching of word and object is still developing, especially past 10.
mis.fix: Have students push each counter across a line or into a cup as they say each number, one word per push.

cra.c: Students count forward and backward to 20 while moving counters along a ten frame pair or stacking and unstacking linking cubes one at a time.
cra.r: Students touch each square on a 0–20 number path as they count forward, then start at a given number and count back, sliding a marker one space per number.
cra.a: Students count forward and backward to 20 without objects, starting from any number the teacher names, and write or point to the numeral where they stopped.
cra.look: Students count aloud while moving one object or one finger per number, and count backward along a number path from a starting point other than 20.

assess: Start at 7 and count to 15. What number did you stop on?
Count back from 18. Where do you stop if you take 5 steps?
advance: What number comes right before 13? How do you know without starting at 1?
Can you count back from 20 to 11 without looking at the number path?

assess: Show me where 12 is on the number path. Count forward from there.
Count your cubes as you take them off the tower one at a time.
advance: Which number comes after 19?
Close your eyes and count back from 10. Then try from 14.

assess: Point to each counter as you count it.
What number comes after 5?
advance: Start at 8 and count to 12 with me.
Count back from 6 to 1.
support: Count with a small set of counters to 10 first, then add a second ten frame for the teens.
Use a short number path from 0 to 10 and count with the student, touching each number together.

d: Count forward and backward to at least 20 with and without objects.

mis.m: Writes teen numbers in reverse order, such as writing 61 for sixteen, because 'six' is heard first.
mis.why: The spoken teen names say the ones before the teen, but the written numeral puts the 1 first.
mis.fix: Build the number on a full ten frame plus extra counters and write the 1 for the full ten first, then the ones.

mis.m: Writes numerals backward, such as a reversed 3, 7 or 9.
mis.why: Letter and numeral formation is still developing, and reversals are common at this age.
mis.fix: Use a number path or numeral strip on each desk and have students trace the numeral with a finger before writing it.

mis.m: Reads 0 as 'nothing' and does not show it with objects or pictures.
mis.why: Students think zero is not a number because there is nothing to count.
mis.fix: Show an empty ten frame and say 'There are zero counters.' Write 0 beside it and place 0 at the start of the number path.

cra.c: Students build numbers 0–20 with counters on ten frames or linking cube trains and match each set to a numeral card.
cra.r: Students draw dots or circles on blank ten frames to show a number and write the numeral beside the drawing, and find the number on a 0–20 number path.
cra.a: Students read and write numerals 0–20 without objects, saying the number aloud and matching the numeral to the number word.
cra.look: Students match numeral cards to ten frame sets and drawings, and write teen numbers by first showing the full ten frame and then the extra ones.

assess: Read this number. How do you know it says 17?
Show me 14 in a different way.
advance: How are 4 and 14 the same and how are they different?
Write the number that is one full ten frame and 6 more.

assess: Show me 11 on the ten frames. How many full ten frames do you have?
Which numeral card matches your drawing?
advance: Draw 18 on the ten frames. How many dots are not in the full frame?
Where is 16 on the number path?

assess: Show me 5 counters.
Point to the number 8.
advance: Write the number for this ten frame.
Show me zero on the ten frame.
support: Give numeral cards 0–10 with dot pictures on the back for self-checking.
Provide tracing strips with the numerals 0–20 and a starting dot on each.

stems: One full ten and ___ more is ___.
d: Read, write, and represent whole numbers from 0 to at least 20 with and without objects or pictures.

mis.m: Counts a set of 8 correctly but, when asked 'How many?', recounts from 1 instead of saying 8.
mis.why: The student has not yet connected the last number said to the total of the set.
mis.fix: After counting, cover the set with a cup and ask 'How many are under the cup?' so the student must use the last number said.

mis.m: Recounts a set after it is spread out or rearranged, believing the total may have changed.
mis.why: Students think the number depends on how long the line looks or how the objects are spaced.
mis.fix: Count a set, spread it out while students watch, and ask 'Did we add any? Did we take any away? So how many now?'

mis.m: Counts some objects twice or skips some when the objects are in a scattered pile.
mis.why: Students lack a system for tracking which objects have already been counted.
mis.fix: Teach students to move each counter to a ten frame or across a line as it is counted.

cra.c: Students count up to 20 counters, bears or cubes by moving each one into a ten frame or a cup, then tell how many in all.
cra.r: Students count pictures of objects in rows, circles and scattered arrangements, marking each one as they count and writing the total.
cra.a: Students tell the total of a set after it is rearranged without recounting, saying 'It is still ___ because we did not add or take away.'
cra.look: Students move objects as they count, say the last number as the total, and keep the same number when the set is spread out or pushed together.

assess: You counted 13. If I move them into a circle, how many will there be?
How do you know you did not count any twice?
advance: If I put these 15 in a long line and those 15 in a pile, which has more?
What is a fast way to count these 18 so you do not lose your place?

assess: How many are in your ten frame now?
I spread out your counters. How many are there?
advance: Count them a new way. Do you get the same number?
Put them in a tower. How many cubes are in the tower?

assess: Touch and count each bear.
How many bears in all?
advance: I hid them under the cup. How many are under there?
Move one at a time into the ten frame as you count.
support: Start with sets of 5 or fewer and add more as the student holds the last number said.
Give a mat with a start line and a finish line so each counted object is moved across.

d: Count a set of objects up to at least 20 and demonstrate that the last number said tells the number of objects in the set regardless of their arrangement or order.

mis.m: Counts each dot one by one on a dot card of 4 instead of seeing the 4 at once.
mis.why: The student has not yet built mental pictures of small quantities.
mis.fix: Flash dot cards and ten frames for two seconds, then hide them, so students practice seeing the quantity without time to count.

mis.m: Recognizes 5 in the standard dice pattern but not when 5 dots are scattered.
mis.why: Students memorize one familiar arrangement instead of seeing the quantity.
mis.fix: Show the same number in several arrangements on dot cards and ask 'How did you see it?' to grow flexible pictures.

mis.m: Says 6 for a scattered set of 5 because the set looks large.
mis.why: Students guess from how much space the dots take up.
mis.fix: After each quick flash, show the card again and count to check, then ask students to describe the groups they saw.

cra.c: Students roll number cubes, flip dot cards and look at quick flashes of counters on five frames and ten frames, then show the number with fingers.
cra.r: Students match dot cards with organized and scattered arrangements to five frames and ten frames, and draw what they saw after a quick look.
cra.a: Students say the number they see in a quick flash and write the numeral, explaining the small groups they saw, such as '3 and 2'.
cra.look: Students say the number of dots without counting one by one after a quick look, and explain the parts they saw.

assess: How did you know it was 6 so fast?
What groups did you see in this card?
advance: Can you see this 7 in a different way?
How many empty spaces are on this five frame?

assess: I flashed the five frame. How many dots?
How many dots on this scattered card?
advance: Draw what you saw on your five frame.
Show me 4 dots in a different arrangement.

assess: How many dots? Do not count.
Show me with your fingers.
advance: I see 2 and 2. How many is that?
Find the card with 3 dots.
support: Use dot cards with only 1–5 dots in dice patterns before adding scattered arrangements.
Show a five frame for a longer look and gradually shorten the time.

d: Recognize instantly the quantity of a small group of objects in organized and random arrangements.

mis.m: Makes a set that is 'more than 6' by adding a much larger number of counters without checking, then cannot explain why it is more.
mis.why: Students think 'more' means 'a lot' instead of comparing to a specific number.
mis.fix: Line up both sets side by side in linking cube trains so students can see the extra cubes on one train.

mis.m: Builds a set that 'looks' bigger by spreading it out, even though it has fewer objects.
mis.why: Students judge quantity by length or space instead of number.
mis.fix: Have students match objects one-to-one with the given set to check which set has extras.

mis.m: Builds a set equal to 9 but miscounts and makes 8, then says it is equal.
mis.why: Counting errors past 5 lead to wrong comparisons.
mis.fix: Build both sets on ten frames so equal sets fill the same squares and differences are easy to see.

cra.c: Students build sets with counters or linking cubes that are more than, less than and equal to a given number up to 20, matching one-to-one with the teacher's set.
cra.r: Students draw sets on ten frames or as dot pictures that are more than, less than or equal to a given numeral, and circle the extra dots on the larger set.
cra.a: Students name a number that is more than, less than or equal to a given number and tell how they know using the number path.
cra.look: Students build cube trains side by side, match objects one-to-one and use the words 'more', 'less' and 'equal' to describe their sets.

assess: How do you know your set is less than 12?
Can you make a set more than 15 using only one more counter?
advance: Make a set that is equal to mine but looks different. Is it still equal?
How many more counters would make your set equal to 17?

assess: Show me a set that is more than 8 on your ten frames.
Which cubes on your train are the extra ones?
advance: Draw a set that is less than 14. How do you know?
Where are both numbers on the number path?

assess: Make 5 cubes like mine.
Is your train longer or shorter?
advance: Add one more cube. Is it more than 5 now?
Take one away. Is it less now?
support: Keep the given number at 10 or less and build both sets on ten frames.
Line up two cube trains next to each other so students can see the difference.

d: Generate a set using concrete and pictorial models that represents a number that is more than, less than, and equal to a given number up to 20.

mis.m: Says one more than 9 is 11, skipping 10.
mis.why: Students count on from the given number but include the given number as the first count.
mis.fix: Use a number path and have the student put a finger on 9, then jump one space and read the number.

mis.m: Says one less than 15 is 16.
mis.why: Students confuse 'less' and 'more', or always move forward on the count sequence.
mis.fix: Act it out with a cube train: show 15, take one cube off, and count what is left.

mis.m: Counts all from 1 to find one more than 17 instead of using the count sequence.
mis.why: The student does not yet see that one more is the next counting number.
mis.fix: Build 17 on two ten frames, add one counter, and ask 'Which number comes next when we count?'

cra.c: Students build a number with counters or linking cubes, add one or take one away, and say the new number.
cra.r: Students use a 0–20 number path to move one space forward for one more and one space back for one less, and draw one more or one less dot on a ten frame.
cra.a: Students name the number that is one more or one less than a given numeral without objects and write the numeral.
cra.look: Students add or remove one cube from a train, hop one space on the number path and name the new number.

assess: What is one more than 19? How do you know?
What is one less than 11?
advance: Which number is one more than 13 and one less than 15?
If one more is 18, what was the first number?

assess: Show me one more than 12 on the number path.
Take one cube off your train of 16. How many now?
advance: Draw one less on your ten frame. What number is it?
How does the number path help you find one less?

assess: Here is 6. Add one cube. How many now?
Point to 9. What number comes next?
advance: Take one away from 7. How many now?
Which number comes before 4?
support: Begin with numbers to 10 on a single ten frame.
Use a number path with arrows marked 'one more' and 'one less'.

d: Generate a number that is one more than or one less than another number up to at least 20.

mis.m: Says a set of 10 small beads is less than a set of 8 large blocks.
mis.why: Students compare by size of objects or space taken instead of number.
mis.fix: Match the two sets one-to-one by lining them up and ask 'Which set has some left over?'

mis.m: Compares two sets of 14 and 15 only by looking and guesses which is more.
mis.why: Students rely on visual estimation when sets are close in size.
mis.fix: Have students count each set onto ten frames and compare the extra counters.

mis.m: Uses 'bigger' or 'taller' instead of 'more' or 'fewer' to compare sets.
mis.why: Everyday language for size is mixed with language for quantity.
mis.fix: Post sentence stems with 'more than', 'fewer than' and 'the same as', and model each one with real sets.

cra.c: Students compare two sets of counters, bears or cubes up to 20 by matching one-to-one or building cube trains side by side.
cra.r: Students draw lines to match objects in two pictures and draw both sets on ten frames to compare.
cra.a: Students say which set has more, fewer or the same using a full sentence and the number of each set.
cra.look: Students match objects one-to-one, line up cube trains and use 'more than', 'fewer than' and 'the same as' in full sentences.

assess: How do you know this set has fewer?
How many more does the bigger set have?
advance: Could a set of 12 large blocks have fewer than a set of 15 small beads? Why?
What could you do to make the sets the same?

assess: Show me how you matched the bears.
Which ten frame has more counters?
advance: How many extra counters are there?
Draw a set with fewer than this one.

assess: Which pile has more?
Line them up. Which line has extras?
advance: Are these the same? How do you know?
Show me the set with fewer.
support: Compare small sets up to 10 that are very different before moving to close numbers.
Give a matching mat with two rows of boxes so objects line up.

d: Compare sets of objects up to at least 20 in each set using comparative language.

mis.m: Says 9 is greater than 12 because 9 is a 'big' digit.
mis.why: Students look at the size of the digit instead of the value of the whole numeral.
mis.fix: Find both numbers on a number path and remind students that numbers farther along the path are greater.

mis.m: Says 16 is less than 13 because 6 comes before 3 when saying 'sixteen' and 'thirteen'.
mis.why: Teen numbers are hard to compare by sound alone.
mis.fix: Build both teen numbers with a full ten frame and extra counters, then compare the extra counters.

mis.m: Uses 'more' and 'less' correctly with objects but cannot compare written numerals without building them.
mis.why: The link between the numeral and its place on the count sequence is not yet strong.
mis.fix: Have students locate each numeral on the number path and say which one they reach first when counting.

cra.c: Students build two given numerals with counters on ten frames and compare the sets before naming which numeral is greater or less.
cra.r: Students find both numerals on a 0–20 number path and color them, then say which comes later in counting.
cra.a: Students compare two numerals up to 20 without objects using 'greater than', 'less than' and 'equal to'.
cra.look: Students point to numerals on the number path, build teen numbers on ten frames and say full comparison sentences.

assess: Which is greater, 17 or 14? How do you know?
How can the number path help you compare?
advance: Name a number that is greater than 11 and less than 15.
Is 19 greater or less than 9? Prove it with a ten frame.

assess: Find 8 and 13 on the number path. Which comes later?
Build 15 and 12. Which has more extra counters?
advance: Which numeral card is less? Tell me with a sentence.
Put these three numerals in order from least to greatest.

assess: Point to 6 and 9. Which is greater?
Which number comes first when we count?
advance: Is 10 greater or less than 7?
Show me both numbers on the ten frame.
support: Compare numerals to 10 first, then move to teen numbers.
Use a number path with numerals and matching dot pictures.

d: Use comparative language to describe two numbers up to 20 presented as written numerals.

mis.m: Finds only one way to make 7, such as 6 and 1, and stops.
mis.why: Students think there is just one correct answer.
mis.fix: Use a shake-and-spill game with two-color counters and record each new pair on a chart.

mis.m: When decomposing 8 into 5 and 3, then says the total changed when the parts are moved apart.
mis.why: Students do not yet see that the parts make the same whole.
mis.fix: Snap two cube trains together and pull them apart while saying '5 and 3 is 8. 8 is 5 and 3.'

mis.m: Lists 4 and 4 as a way to make 9.
mis.why: Counting errors or guessing lead to parts that do not match the whole.
mis.fix: Have students build each pair on a ten frame and count the total to check.

cra.c: Students break linking cube trains, spill two-color counters and fill five frames and ten frames to find all the ways to make numbers up to 10.
cra.r: Students draw two-color dots on ten frames and draw number bonds with circles to show the parts and whole.
cra.a: Students say and write pairs that make a number up to 10 and tell the missing part when one part is hidden.
cra.look: Students break cube trains into two parts, spill counters and draw number bonds showing different ways to make a number.

assess: How many ways can you make 10? How do you know you found them all?
If one part is 3, what is the other part of 8?
advance: How are 4 and 6 and 6 and 4 the same?
If I hide some counters and show 2, and the whole is 9, how many are hiding?

assess: Show me 7 on your ten frame in two colors.
Draw a number bond for your cube train.
advance: Find another way to make 7.
What is the missing part in this number bond?

assess: Break your 5 train into two parts.
How many red and how many yellow?
advance: Is 3 and 2 the same as 5?
Make 5 a different way.
support: Start with numbers to 5 on a five frame.
Use two colors of cubes so each part is easy to see.

d: Compose and decompose numbers up to 10 with objects and pictures.

mis.m: Acts out 'joining' by moving counters into one group, then counts only the new counters as the total.
mis.why: Students focus on the last action and forget the first group.
mis.fix: Have students count the first group, add the new ones, then count all together on a ten frame.

mis.m: Puts all the counters together when the story is about taking some away.
mis.why: Students do not yet link the story action to joining or separating.
mis.fix: Act out the story with students as the characters and ask 'Did more come or did some leave?'

mis.m: Shows separating but keeps the removed counters on the mat and counts them in the result.
mis.why: Students do not show that the removed objects are gone.
mis.fix: Use a 'gone' cup or cross off drawn objects so removed items are out of the count.

cra.c: Students act out join and separate stories with counters, linking cubes and their own bodies, putting groups together and taking some away.
cra.r: Students draw joining and separating stories with pictures, using arrows to show joining and crossing off to show taking away.
cra.a: Students match the action to the words 'add' and 'take away' and say a number sentence, connecting the plus and minus signs to the actions they showed.
cra.look: Students physically join and separate groups and say whether their story is adding or taking away.

assess: Is this a joining story or a separating story? How do you know?
What changed when the bunnies hopped away?
advance: Tell me a story where some leave. What will happen to the group?
Can you make a joining story with 4 and 3?

assess: Show me how your drawing shows joining.
Which counters left in your story?
advance: Draw a separating story with 7 apples.
Say a number sentence for your picture.

assess: Put these two groups together.
Take two away. How many left?
advance: Did more come or did some leave?
Show me with the cubes.
support: Act out stories with students as characters before using counters.
Give a story mat with a 'join' side and a 'take away' cup.

d: Model the action of joining to represent addition and the action of separating to represent subtraction.

mis.m: Adds both numbers in a take-away story because the student sees two numbers.
mis.why: Students grab numbers without making sense of the story action.
mis.fix: Retell the story with a picture and ask 'Are we getting more or fewer?' before solving.

mis.m: Counts the total in a joining story but leaves out one of the starting objects.
mis.why: Counting is not yet organized when objects are moved quickly.
mis.fix: Have students place objects on a ten frame so every counter has a spot.

mis.m: Draws detailed pictures and runs out of time before solving.
mis.why: Students think a math drawing must look like a real picture.
mis.fix: Model quick math drawings with circles or dots and say 'Math pictures can be simple.'

cra.c: Students solve word problems by acting them out with counters, linking cubes or small toys on a story mat, using sums up to 10 and differences within 10.
cra.r: Students draw circles or dots for the story, cross off for taking away, and show the answer on a ten frame or number path.
cra.a: Students say a number sentence for the story and connect each number to part of their drawing.
cra.look: Students act out word problems with objects or quick drawings and point to the answer in their model.

assess: How did you know to add?
How does your drawing show the story?
advance: Change the story so the answer is 6. What did you change?
Can you solve it a different way?

assess: Show me the 4 birds in your drawing.
Where are the ones that flew away?
advance: Use the number path to check your answer.
Say a number sentence for your picture.

assess: How many frogs at the start?
Did more come or did some leave?
advance: Show me with counters.
How many now?
support: Read the story slowly and act out each part with real objects.
Give a ten frame mat with the starting number already shown.

d: Solve word problems using objects and drawings to find sums up to 10 and differences within 10.

mis.m: Says 'I just knew' or 'I counted' without telling what was counted or how.
mis.why: Students are not yet used to explaining their thinking.
mis.fix: Model think-alouds: 'I had 5, I counted on 6, 7, so I have 7' and have partners repeat.

mis.m: Writes a number sentence that does not match the story, such as 5 + 2 for a take-away story.
mis.why: Students see plus as the only way to write a number sentence.
mis.fix: Have students point to each part of the drawing as they say each number and sign in the sentence.

mis.m: Counts all from 1 every time and cannot describe counting on.
mis.why: Counting on is not yet developed and counting all feels safe.
mis.fix: Start with the larger number in a cup or under a hand, say it, and count on the rest.

cra.c: Students use counters, ten frames and fingers to solve adding and subtracting problems within 10 and show a partner how they solved it.
cra.r: Students draw pictures, ten frames or number path jumps to show their strategy and point to them while explaining.
cra.a: Students say and write a number sentence that matches their strategy and explain each number and sign.
cra.look: Students explain their strategy to a partner while pointing to their objects or drawing, and match their work to a number sentence.

assess: How did you solve it? Tell me each step.
How is your way the same as your partner's way?
advance: Can you solve it a faster way?
Which way do you think is easier? Why?

assess: Show me how your drawing matches your number sentence.
Where did you start on the number path?
advance: What does the plus sign mean in your story?
Could you count on instead of counting all?

assess: What did you do first?
Show me with your counters.
advance: Point to the 3 in your picture.
How many now?
support: Give a partner talk card with 'First', 'Then' and 'So' picture prompts.
Model one strategy and have the student copy it with counters.

d: Explain the strategies used to solve problems involving adding and subtracting within 10 using spoken words, concrete and pictorial models, and number sentences.

mis.m: Calls a dime a nickel because a nickel is bigger.
mis.why: Students link size to name or value and the dime is the smallest coin.
mis.fix: Use magnifiers to look at the pictures on each coin and sort coins by the picture on the back and front.

mis.m: Confuses pennies and nickels, or calls every coin 'money'.
mis.why: Students do not have names for each coin and have not noticed color and edge differences.
mis.fix: Do a coin sort by color first, then by size, then by the picture, naming each coin aloud.

mis.m: Names the quarter correctly only when it is face-up.
mis.why: Students learn one side of a coin and do not recognize the other side.
mis.fix: Show both sides of each coin on an anchor chart and play a flip-and-name game.

cra.c: Students sort real or play pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters by color, size and pictures, and do coin rubbings with crayons.
cra.r: Students match coin pictures to names on a sorting mat and draw each coin with its key features, such as copper color for the penny or ridged edge for the dime.
cra.a: Students name each coin when it is held up and match coin names to the coin, using only the names penny, nickel, dime and quarter.
cra.look: Students sort coins, look closely with magnifiers, describe color, size, edge and pictures, and name each coin.

assess: How do you know this is a dime and not a penny?
What is on the back of the quarter?
advance: Which coins have smooth edges and which have bumpy edges?
How are a nickel and a quarter alike and different?

assess: Sort these coins into groups. Tell me your groups.
Find the coin with the person facing left.
advance: Which coin is the smallest? What is its name?
Flip this coin. Is it still a nickel?

assess: Which coin is brown?
Point to the quarter.
advance: Is this a penny or a nickel?
Find another dime.
support: Start with two coins, penny and quarter, then add one coin at a time.
Use an anchor chart showing both sides of each coin with its name.

d: Identify U.S. coins by name, including pennies, nickels, dimes, and quarters.

mis.m: Counts by ones to 29, then says 'twenty-ten'.
mis.why: Students apply the ones pattern past 9 instead of moving to the next decade.
mis.fix: Count with a hundred chart or a 0–100 number path and pause at each row end to name the next ten.

mis.m: Counts by tens from 10 correctly but cannot start at 30 or 50.
mis.why: Students learned the decade sequence only as a chant from the beginning.
mis.fix: Start counts at different decade numbers using a ten-stick or bundle of ten for each count.

mis.m: Counts by ones but skips numbers in the 70s or 90s, or confuses seventy and seventeen.
mis.why: Decade names and teen names sound alike.
mis.fix: Contrast 17 and 70 with a single ten-stick plus 7 cubes and seven ten-sticks.

cra.c: Students count by tens using bundles of ten straws or linking cube trains of ten, and count by ones with loose cubes from a given number.
cra.r: Students point to numbers on a hundred chart or 0–100 number path as they count by ones or tens from any starting number.
cra.a: Students recite counts by ones and tens from a starting number without objects, saying where the next decade begins.
cra.look: Students count aloud from different starting numbers, touching numbers on a hundred chart and moving ten-sticks for counting by tens.

assess: Start at 46 and count to 55. What comes after 49?
Count by tens from 30. Where do you stop?
advance: What comes after 69? How do you know?
What number comes after 100?

assess: Touch each number on the hundred chart as you count from 23.
Count the bundles of ten: 10, 20, ...
advance: Find 80 on the hundred chart. What comes before it when we count by tens?
Count by ones from 88 to 101.

assess: Count with me from 1 to 20.
Count the ten-sticks by tens.
advance: What comes after 29?
Start at 10 and count by tens.
support: Use a 1–30 number path before moving to the hundred chart.
Count by tens with ten-sticks so each word matches a bundle.

d: Recite numbers up to at least 100 by ones and tens beginning with any given number.

mis.m: Says a triangle that is turned upside down or is long and thin is not a triangle.
mis.why: Students have seen mostly upright, equal-sided triangles.
mis.fix: Show many triangles in different sizes and positions and count the sides and corners each time.

mis.m: Says a square is not a rectangle.
mis.why: Students think rectangles must be long and squares are a separate group.
mis.fix: Check a square for rectangle features: 4 sides, 4 square corners. Say 'A square is a special rectangle.'

mis.m: Calls an oval a circle.
mis.why: Students group round shapes together without looking closely.
mis.fix: Compare a circle and an oval side by side and fold a paper circle to show it is the same all the way around.

cra.c: Students hold and trace 2D shape sets, including tilted triangles, long rectangles and squares, and go on a shape hunt in the classroom.
cra.r: Students draw and sort pictures of circles, triangles, rectangles and squares in different sizes and positions.
cra.a: Students name shapes and explain using sides and corners, saying 'A square is a special rectangle.'
cra.look: Students turn shapes in their hands, count sides and corners and name shapes in any position.

assess: How do you know this is a triangle even though it is upside down?
Why is a square also a rectangle?
advance: Is every rectangle a square? Show me.
Draw a triangle that looks very different from mine.

assess: Count the sides on this shape.
Find all the rectangles on this page.
advance: Is this oval a circle? How do you know?
Turn the triangle. Is it still a triangle?

assess: Point to the circle.
How many sides does this shape have?
advance: Find a square.
Is this a triangle?
support: Start with one shape at a time and many examples of it.
Use shapes with sides marked in color to help count.

d: Identify two-dimensional shapes, including circles, triangles, rectangles, and squares as special rectangles.

mis.m: Calls a ball a circle or a can a rectangle.
mis.why: Students use 2D names for 3D objects.
mis.fix: Hold up a flat circle and a ball side by side and ask 'Which one is flat? Which can you hold all around?'

mis.m: Says a cone on its side is not a cone.
mis.why: Students recognize solids only in familiar positions.
mis.fix: Turn cone and cylinder models in different directions and ask students to name them each time.

mis.m: Calls a box shaped like a rectangle a cube.
mis.why: Students think all boxes are cubes.
mis.fix: Compare a cube and a long box and check whether all the faces are the same square.

cra.c: Students handle 3D solid sets and real objects such as cans, balls, party hats and number cubes, and sort them into cylinders, cones, spheres and cubes.
cra.r: Students draw or cut out pictures of real objects and glue them under labeled 3D solids.
cra.a: Students name real-world examples of each solid and explain using words like 'rolls', 'stacks', 'flat' and 'curved'.
cra.look: Students hold real objects, roll and stack them and name each as a cylinder, cone, sphere or cube.

assess: Why is this can a cylinder?
How is a sphere different from a circle?
advance: Find something in our room that is a cone.
Which solids can roll and stack? Why?

assess: Sort these objects. Tell me your groups.
Which object is a sphere?
advance: Is this box a cube? How do you know?
Draw something at home that is a cylinder.

assess: Which one is the ball?
Point to the cube.
advance: Does it roll?
Is this a cone?
support: Use only two solids at a time, such as sphere and cube.
Show a picture card for each solid next to a real object.

stems: I see a ___ in our room.
d: Identify three-dimensional solids, including cylinders, cones, spheres, and cubes, in the real world.

mis.m: Says a cube has a 'square' but does not see that every face is a square.
mis.why: Students name only the face they look at.
mis.fix: Have students trace each face of a cube on paper and count the squares.

mis.m: Says a cylinder has rectangles on its ends.
mis.why: Students mix up the curved side and the flat ends.
mis.fix: Stamp the end of a cylinder in paint or trace it to show the flat face is a circle.

mis.m: Says a sphere has a circle face.
mis.why: Students know a sphere looks round and think it has a flat face.
mis.fix: Try to trace a sphere and talk about why there is no flat face to trace.

cra.c: Students press 3D solids into play dough or paint and trace faces on paper to find the 2D shapes.
cra.r: Students match drawings of solids to drawings of their faces and draw the shapes they traced.
cra.a: Students name the 2D shape that makes a face of a solid and explain, such as 'The cube has square faces.'
cra.look: Students trace or print faces of solids and name the flat shapes they see.

assess: What flat shapes did you find on the cylinder?
Why can't you trace a sphere?
advance: Which solid has only square faces?
If a face is a circle, which solids could it be?

assess: Trace a face of the cube. What shape is it?
Match this print to the solid it came from.
advance: How many faces can you trace on the cube?
What shape is the bottom of the cone?

assess: Point to the flat part.
Is it a circle or a square?
advance: Trace it with your finger.
Find a circle on the cylinder.
support: Start with a cube and a cylinder only.
Provide large solids so tracing is easy.

d: Identify two-dimensional components of three-dimensional objects.

mis.m: Describes a shape by color or size, such as 'It is the big red one.'
mis.why: Students notice the features that stand out instead of math attributes.
mis.fix: Use shapes that are all the same color and model describing sides, corners and edges.

mis.m: Uses 'corners' but not 'vertices', or uses 'points' only.
mis.why: Students know informal words but have not linked them to formal words.
mis.fix: Post an anchor chart pairing words such as 'corner' and 'vertex', 'side' and 'edge', and use both in every talk.

mis.m: Counts the same corner twice when counting vertices.
mis.why: Students lack a way to keep track around a shape.
mis.fix: Mark a starting corner with a dot or sticker and count around until returning to it.

cra.c: Students trace sides with fingers, put sticky dots on vertices and use straws or sticks to model sides of 2D shapes.
cra.r: Students draw shapes and mark corners with dots and sides with color, then label the number of each.
cra.a: Students describe shapes using both informal and formal words, such as 'corners' and 'vertices', and 'flat' and 'two-dimensional'.
cra.look: Students count sides and vertices, mark them on drawings, and use both everyday and math words.

assess: How many vertices does this shape have? How do you know?
What is another word for corner?
advance: How are a triangle and a rectangle alike and different?
Describe this shape without saying its name.

assess: Put a dot on each vertex.
Color each side a different color.
advance: How many sides and vertices does a square have?
Which shape has no vertices?

assess: Show me a corner.
Count the sides.
advance: Is this side straight or curved?
How many corners?
support: Use large shapes and sticky dots for corners.
Give a word card pairing 'corner' with 'vertex'.

d: Identify attributes of two-dimensional shapes using informal and formal geometric language interchangeably.

mis.m: Sorts shapes by color or size instead of by the number of sides or vertices.
mis.why: Color and size are easier to see than math attributes.
mis.fix: Give shapes in one color and ask 'How else could we sort them?'

mis.m: Puts a tilted square in a different group from an upright square.
mis.why: Students think turning a shape changes it.
mis.fix: Turn shapes while students watch and ask 'Did it change? Is it still a square?'

mis.m: Leaves out irregular shapes, such as a scalene triangle or a long thin rectangle, because they do not 'look right'.
mis.why: Students have seen only typical shapes.
mis.fix: Include many irregular shapes and check each one by its attributes.

cra.c: Students sort 2D shape sets and 3D solids of many sizes, positions and regular and irregular forms into labeled hoops or trays.
cra.r: Students sort and glue shape pictures into a sorting chart and draw one more example for each group.
cra.a: Students name their sorting rule and tell why each shape belongs, using the number of sides, vertices, faces, or whether it rolls or stacks.
cra.look: Students sort shapes by attributes, tell their sorting rule and explain how turned or irregular shapes still belong.

assess: What is your sorting rule?
Why does this skinny triangle go with the triangles?
advance: Can you sort these shapes a different way?
Which shape could go in two groups?

assess: Tell me why this shape goes here.
Find all the shapes with 4 sides.
advance: Sort the solids by ones that roll and ones that stack.
Draw one more shape for this group.

assess: Put all the circles here.
Is this a triangle?
advance: Does it have 3 sides?
Turn it. Is it still a triangle?
support: Give only two groups to sort into with a picture label.
Use shapes in one color so students focus on sides and corners.

d: Classify and sort a variety of regular and irregular two- and three-dimensional figures regardless of orientation or size.

mis.m: Builds a 'triangle' with sticks that do not meet at the corners.
mis.why: Students do not yet know that sides must connect to close the shape.
mis.fix: Have students trace around their built shape with a finger and check that there are no gaps.

mis.m: Draws a square with sides that are clearly different lengths.
mis.why: Fine motor skills and attention to equal sides are developing.
mis.fix: Use geoboards or dot paper so students can count equal spaces for each side.

mis.m: Makes a shape with curved sides and calls it a rectangle.
mis.why: Students focus on the number of sides and not on straight sides.
mis.fix: Compare straws, which are straight, with yarn, which curves, and ask which one makes a rectangle.

cra.c: Students create 2D shapes using straws, craft sticks, play dough, yarn, geoboards and pattern blocks.
cra.r: Students draw shapes on dot paper and plain paper, then label the number of sides and vertices.
cra.a: Students name the shape they created and explain how they made it, using sides and vertices.
cra.look: Students build closed shapes with straight or curved materials and tell how many sides and vertices they used.

assess: How did you make your rectangle? What did you check?
Why is your shape closed?
advance: Make a different triangle with the same sticks.
Can you make a square using two triangles?

assess: Draw a triangle on your dot paper. How many dots did you use for corners?
Show me the sides of your shape.
advance: Make a rectangle that is not a square.
Draw a circle and a square next to each other.

assess: Make a triangle with 3 sticks.
Do the sticks touch?
advance: Trace around your shape.
How many sides did you use?
support: Give the exact number of sticks needed for the shape.
Provide a shape outline to build on top of.

d: Create two-dimensional shapes using a variety of materials and drawings.

mis.m: Names color or shape as something to measure.
mis.why: Students describe what they notice instead of measurable attributes.
mis.fix: Sort words into 'can measure' and 'cannot measure' and model length, capacity and weight with real objects.

mis.m: Uses 'big' for all attributes instead of 'long', 'heavy' or 'holds more'.
mis.why: Students use one general word for size.
mis.fix: Model precise words with real objects: 'This rope is long. This rock is heavy. This cup holds more.'

mis.m: Thinks a taller container always holds more.
mis.why: Students judge capacity by height alone.
mis.fix: Fill a tall thin container and a short wide one with rice or water and pour to compare.

cra.c: Students explore length with ribbons and cubes, capacity with cups and rice or water, and weight with balance scales and classroom objects.
cra.r: Students draw an object and draw arrows or pictures to show its length, what it can hold and how heavy it feels.
cra.a: Students name a measurable attribute using words such as 'long', 'tall', 'holds' and 'heavy'.
cra.look: Students hold, fill and compare real objects and name length, capacity or weight with precise words.

assess: What could we measure about this water bottle?
How is length different from weight?
advance: Name an object where we can measure length, capacity and weight.
Can we measure color? Why not?

assess: Show me the length of this pencil with your fingers.
What does this cup hold?
advance: Which word tells about weight?
Draw something heavy and something light.

assess: Is this long or short?
Is this heavy or light?
advance: What can this cup hold?
Show me how long it is.
support: Focus on one attribute per day with real objects.
Use picture cards for long, heavy and holds more.

d: Give an example of a measurable attribute of a given object, including length, capacity, and weight.

mis.m: Compares the lengths of two pencils without lining up their ends.
mis.why: Students do not yet know objects must start at the same place.
mis.fix: Line both objects up on a starting line and then compare the other ends.

mis.m: Says a large, light object is heavier than a small, heavy object.
mis.why: Students judge weight by size.
mis.fix: Use a balance scale and ask students to predict, then test.

mis.m: Says one object is longer but cannot describe the difference.
mis.why: Students name which one is more but not how much more.
mis.fix: Lay linking cubes beside the extra part and say 'It is 3 cubes longer.'

cra.c: Students compare two objects using balance scales, linking cube trains for length and pouring rice or water for capacity.
cra.r: Students draw two objects side by side on a starting line and color the extra part, or draw a balance scale with the heavier side down.
cra.a: Students say which object has more or less of an attribute and describe the difference, such as 'The pencil is 2 cubes longer.'
cra.look: Students line up objects, use balance scales and pour to compare, and tell which has more or less and by how much.

assess: How do you know the crayon is shorter?
Which holds more? How much more?
advance: How could you compare two things that are across the room?
Is the bigger box always heavier? Test it.

assess: Show me the starting line.
Which side of the balance went down?
advance: How many cubes longer is it?
Draw what you saw on the balance scale.

assess: Which one is longer?
Which one is heavier?
advance: Line them up. Which is longer now?
Which cup holds more?
support: Compare objects that are very different first.
Use a mat with a starting line and a balance picture.

d: Compare two objects with a common measurable attribute to see which object has more of/less of the attribute and describe the difference.

mis.m: Sorts objects into groups that overlap, putting one object in two groups.
mis.why: Students do not yet use one clear sorting rule.
mis.fix: Name one rule at a time and have students check each object by the rule.

mis.m: Mixes up categories partway, such as switching from color to size.
mis.why: Students forget the rule while sorting.
mis.fix: Label each group with a picture card and say the rule aloud before each object is placed.

mis.m: Collects data but does not count each group.
mis.why: Students think sorting is the last step.
mis.fix: After sorting, put each group on a ten frame and write how many.

cra.c: Students collect and sort real objects such as buttons, blocks or snack items into two or three labeled trays or hoops.
cra.r: Students draw pictures of sorted groups and use tally marks or ten frames to show how many are in each group.
cra.a: Students tell how many are in each category and name the sorting rule.
cra.look: Students sort objects into labeled groups, count each group and tell the rule.

assess: What is your sorting rule?
How many are in each group?
advance: Can you sort the same objects into three groups?
Which group has the most?

assess: Show me the label for this group.
Count the buttons in the red group.
advance: Draw your groups.
Use tally marks to show how many.

assess: Put the big ones here.
Is this red or blue?
advance: Count this group.
Where does this one go?
support: Start with two groups that are very different.
Use sorting mats with picture labels.

d: Collect, sort, and organize data into two or three categories.

mis.m: Places objects in a real-object graph with uneven spaces, so a shorter column looks taller.
mis.why: Students do not yet know each object needs one space.
mis.fix: Use a graph mat with boxes so each object fills one box.

mis.m: Starts columns at different places on a picture graph.
mis.why: Students do not see the need for a common starting line.
mis.fix: Draw a bold start line and have students place every first picture on it.

mis.m: Leaves out a category label on the graph.
mis.why: Students forget others need to know what each column shows.
mis.fix: Have students name and label each column with a picture or word before placing objects.

cra.c: Students build real-object graphs using shoes, blocks or snacks on a floor graph mat with labeled columns.
cra.r: Students make picture graphs by drawing or gluing one picture per box in labeled columns.
cra.a: Students tell how many are in each column and say what their graph shows.
cra.look: Students place one object or picture per box on a labeled graph mat and start each column on the line.

assess: How did you make sure your graph is fair?
What does each picture stand for?
advance: What label would help someone read your graph?
If one more student chose apples, what would change?

assess: Show me your start line.
Put one picture in each box.
advance: Label each column.
How many pictures are in this column?

assess: Put your shoe in the box.
Which column is this?
advance: Put one in each box.
How many shoes here?
support: Use a two-column graph mat with picture labels.
Place the first object with the student to model.

stems: I put one in each box.
d: Use data to create real-object and picture graphs.

mis.m: Says the column with the biggest pictures has the most.
mis.why: Students judge by picture size instead of number.
mis.fix: Count each column and compare numbers, not size.

mis.m: Reads one column but cannot compare columns.
mis.why: Students see each column alone.
mis.fix: Ask 'Which has more? How many more?' and line up cubes to compare.

mis.m: Makes conclusions not in the graph, such as 'Everyone likes apples.'
mis.why: Students mix their opinions with data.
mis.fix: Point to the graph and ask 'Does the graph show that? Where?'

cra.c: Students read real-object graphs, count each column and line up cubes to compare columns.
cra.r: Students read picture graphs and circle the column with the most and the least.
cra.a: Students say conclusions such as 'More friends like apples than bananas.'
cra.look: Students count columns, point to the graph and say what the graph shows.

assess: What does the graph tell us?
How many more chose apples than bananas?
advance: What question could we answer with this graph?
If 3 more chose bananas, which would have more?

assess: Which column has the most?
Count the pictures in this column.
advance: Which has the fewest?
Are any columns the same?

assess: Point to the tallest column.
How many here?
advance: Which has more?
Count with me.
support: Use graphs with only two columns.
Put cubes next to pictures to count.

d: Draw conclusions from real-object and picture graphs.

mis.m: Thinks money comes from an ATM or a parent's wallet, not from work.
mis.why: Students see where money comes from but not how it is earned.
mis.fix: Read a story about a worker and ask 'How did they get money? They worked.'

mis.m: Lists only one job, such as teacher.
mis.why: Students know only the jobs they see.
mis.fix: Do a community helper walk or picture sort and name ways each person earns income.

mis.m: Says finding money on the ground is earning income.
mis.why: Students mix earning with getting money in other ways.
mis.fix: Sort picture cards into 'worked for it' and 'did not work for it'.

cra.c: Students role-play jobs at a classroom store, bakery or vet clinic using play coins as pay for work done.
cra.r: Students draw a worker and the job they do, and sort job picture cards into a 'ways to earn income' chart.
cra.a: Students say 'People earn income by working' and name a job and the work that is done.
cra.look: Students act out jobs, name ways people earn income and connect pay to work.

assess: How do people earn income?
How does a firefighter earn income?
advance: What job would you like? How would you earn income?
Can a kid earn income? How?

assess: Draw a person working. What is their job?
Sort these pictures. Which show earning income?
advance: Tell me two ways to earn income.
Why does the baker get paid?

assess: Who works here?
What does a doctor do?
advance: Does she get money for working?
Point to a worker.
support: Use picture cards of familiar jobs.
Role-play a simple job with the student.

d: Identify ways to earn income.

mis.m: Says a birthday present of money is income.
mis.why: Students see any money received as the same.
mis.fix: Sort cards with 'Did you work for it?' and model with stories.

mis.m: Says allowance for doing chores is a gift.
mis.why: Students do not connect the chore with earning.
mis.fix: Act out a chore and payment and ask 'What did you do to get it?'

mis.m: Thinks gifts must be wrapped toys and not money.
mis.why: Students link gifts only to presents.
mis.fix: Show a birthday card with money and talk about it as a gift.

cra.c: Students act out short scenes, such as doing chores for coins or getting a birthday card with money, and decide income or gift.
cra.r: Students sort picture cards into 'income' and 'gift' columns.
cra.a: Students say whether money is income or a gift and tell why, such as 'It is income because she worked.'
cra.look: Students sort and act out money stories and tell whether work was done.

assess: Is this income or a gift? How do you know?
What is the difference between income and a gift?
advance: Can the same money be a gift one time and income another time?
Tell me a story about income.

assess: Sort this card. Did he work?
Show me an income card.
advance: Draw a gift of money.
Why is allowance for chores income?

assess: Did she work for it?
Is it a present?
advance: Is this a gift?
Point to the income card.
support: Use only two picture cards at a time.
Ask the single question 'Did they work?' for every card.

d: Differentiate between money received as income and money received as gifts.

mis.m: Says a skill is a tool, such as 'a hammer' for a builder.
mis.why: Students mix up tools and skills.
mis.fix: Sort cards into 'things they use' and 'things they know how to do'.

mis.m: Lists skills that do not match the job.
mis.why: Students do not know the job well.
mis.fix: Watch a short clip or read about a job and list what the worker does.

mis.m: Names only one skill for every job, such as 'being nice'.
mis.why: Students use a general answer.
mis.fix: Ask 'What else must they know how to do?' and list on a chart.

cra.c: Students act out jobs and show skills, such as counting coins at a store or measuring at a bakery.
cra.r: Students draw a worker and pictures of skills, and match job and skill picture cards.
cra.a: Students name a job and list two skills, such as 'A cook must measure and read.'
cra.look: Students act out jobs and name skills each job needs.

assess: What skills does a cashier need?
Why does a nurse need to count?
advance: What skill do you have that helps in a job?
Which jobs need math skills?

assess: Match the skill to the job.
Draw a skill for a teacher.
advance: Name two skills a farmer needs.
Is a hammer a skill or a tool?

assess: What does a cook do?
Can she read?
advance: Point to a skill.
What does he know how to do?
support: Use picture cards of skills.
Act out one job and skill together.

d: List simple skills required for jobs.

mis.m: Says toys and candy are needs.
mis.why: Students think things they want very much are needs.
mis.fix: Ask 'Can you live without it?' and sort cards together.

mis.m: Says all food is a want, including healthy food.
mis.why: Students link 'want' to liking something.
mis.fix: Sort food examples and talk about which keep us healthy.

mis.m: Does not connect income to buying wants and needs.
mis.why: Students do not see how money gets to the store.
mis.fix: Act out earning coins at a job and spending them at the classroom store.

cra.c: Students sort real items or toy items into 'wants' and 'needs' bins and use play coins earned by job tasks to buy items at a classroom store.
cra.r: Students draw or glue pictures of wants and needs in two columns and draw a person earning money to buy a need.
cra.a: Students tell whether an item is a want or a need and explain that income helps people buy wants and needs.
cra.look: Students sort items, explain choices and connect income to buying wants and needs.

assess: Is a coat a want or a need? Why?
How do people get money to buy needs?
advance: Can something be a need for one person and a want for another?
If you have a little money, should you buy a want or a need first?

assess: Sort these cards. Tell me why.
Show me a need.
advance: Draw something you want and something you need.
How did you get coins for the store?

assess: Do we need water?
Is this toy a want?
advance: Can you live without it?
Point to a need.
support: Use a small set of very clear wants and needs.
Use real objects for sorting.

d: Distinguish between wants and needs and identify income as a source to meet one's wants and needs.
